why_angle: The rival answer runs no search, cites no page, and only ever offers bone conduction for running and cycling. It never says that Bluetooth fails underwater, that IP55 headsets like the OpenRun Pro 2 are not for swimming, or that a swimmer needs IP68 plus onboard MP3 storage. Swimming is the one use where bone conduction is the only answer, and this page names the sets that qualify, with dated prices.

page.title: Bone Conduction vs Regular Headphones: Which to Buy (2026)
page.h1: Bone conduction or regular headphones? Which one wins for you
page.desc: Bone conduction or regular headphones? Sealed headphones sound better and cancel noise. Bone conduction keeps your ears open, and only IP68 sets with onboard storage play music while you swim. Prices checked 2026-11-17.
page.answer: Short answer. Bone conduction or headphones: regular headphones win for sound and noise cancelling, and the soundcore Space One runs 40 h with ANC. Bone conduction wins on runs and in the pool, where Bluetooth fails underwater: get IP68 with 32 GB onboard, like the MOJAWA Run Plus.

What the differences mean

  • Weight on your head: the Space One weighs 265 g and the OpenRun Pro 2 weighs 30.3 g. 265 ÷ 30.3 = about 8.7 times the weight.
  • Runtime per charge: 40 h with ANC ÷ 12 h = 3.3 times. soundcore tests at 50% volume and Shokz at 75%, so this is not an equal-volume comparison.
  • Days between charges at 2 h a day: Space One 40 ÷ 2 = 20 days; Purra Swim 15 ÷ 2 = 7.5; OpenRun Pro 2 12 ÷ 2 = 6; Run Plus 8 ÷ 2 = 4.
  • Two bone conduction sets at the same 75% test volume: OpenRun Pro 2 12 h ÷ Run Plus 8 h = 1.5 times as long per charge.
  • Cost of swimming: OpenSwim Pro $229.95 − Run Plus $99.99 = $129.96 more for the same IP68 rating and 32 GB of storage.
  • Sound, measured: SoundGuys scored the sealed Space One 3.8/5 on its MDAQS model and the open-ear AeroFit 2 1.8/5. 3.8 ÷ 1.8 = 2.1 times. SoundGuys could not measure the OpenRun Pro 2's frequency response on its test fixture at all.

Why only some bone conduction headphones work in the pool

Shokz states it plainly: 'water disrupts Bluetooth signals underwater', and 'For underwater listening, MP3 Mode is required.' This is radio physics, not one brand's design. Any headset that only streams from your phone goes silent once your head is underwater. To swim with music you need two things together: an IP68 rating and music stored on the headset.

  • MOJAWA Run Plus: IP68 and 32 GB of MP3 storage. HeadphonesAddict cites MOJAWA's figure of 2 m for up to 2 h underwater.
  • MOJAWA Purra Swim: IP68 to 2 m, 32 GB (MOJAWA says 8,000+ songs) and 15 h. Earplugs come in the box 'for maximum underwater sound quality'.
  • Shokz OpenSwim Pro: IP68 and 32 GB. Shokz rates it at 9 h on Bluetooth but 6 h in MP3 mode, so plan swim time on the 6 h figure.
  • Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 and soundcore AeroFit 2: both IP55. Shokz says the OpenRun Pro 2 'does not have onboard storage' and 'is not intended for swimming'.
  • soundcore Space One: no water rating at all. soundcore advises against using it at the gym.

The Run Plus and Purra Swim charge through MOJAWA's Type-C magnetic cable, not a plain USB-C port, so pack it when you travel (a spare is $15.90). On the regular-headphone side, the Space One cannot enter multipoint pairing while in LDAC mode, and the AeroFit 2's LDAC works only with Android, so iPhone owners get AAC on both. Bone conduction's thinner bass has a mechanical cause. Shokz calls strong vibration 'one of the main criticisms of bone conduction headphones', and the OpenRun Pro 2 hands low frequencies to a separate air-conduction driver.

Not recommended

Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 for anyone who swims. It is a strong road-running set, but it is IP55, has no onboard storage, and Shokz itself says it is not for swimming. Swimmers should pick one of the IP68 sets above. soundcore AeroFit 2 for sound quality: SoundGuys rated it 5.3/10 and did not recommend it. SoundGuys found its response 'severely compromised in all but a small section of the midrange' because the open design has no seal. Buy it for comfort and awareness, not for sound.
